### `AK1` — HELD · PROVEN

**Claim.** the three primitive forms are a universal reversible language: every instance a permutation of order 3, generating A_27

**Argument.** Each form adds a fixed amount mod 3 to one trit under a condition on another, so three applications return every state. Order exactly 3 by construction, which is what makes the inverse derivable and an inverse instruction set unnecessary.

**Measured.** gate_instances: 15; all_permutations: true; all_order_3: true; group_order: 5444434725209176080384000000; A27_computed: 5444434725209176080384000000; equal: true; digits: 28; registration_typed: 5444434725209176080384000 (25 digits)

**Note.** All fifteen gate instances are permutations of the 27 states and every one has order exactly 3, so a program's inverse is that program with each gate applied twice more and THE LANGUAGE NEEDS NO INVERSE INSTRUCTION SET. The group they generate is A_27, agreeing with M's recorded figure from an implementation written separately -- two independent codings landing on one 28-digit number is what makes a re-implementation worth having. ERRATUM, AND THE REASON IT IS ONLY AN ERRATUM: the registration typed A_27 as a 25-digit number, dropping three zeros, so the decimal expansion in the prediction was wrong by a factor of a thousand. The tool COMPUTES 27!/2 rather than comparing against the typed digits, which is why a transcription slip in the registration is a footnote instead of a false verdict. AGENTS.md already says to derive constants and never hardcode them; the tool obeyed it and the prose did not.

### `AK2` — HELD · PROVEN · NOT AT RISK

**Claim.** reversibility is inherited by composition, so every program has in-degree 1 with no analysis

**Not at risk.** A composition of bijections is a bijection, and the registration says so. The manifest's own argument field concedes it: "the 400 sampled were a check on the implementation, never the grounds for the claim".

**Argument.** A composition of bijections is a bijection. Every primitive is a bijection, so in-degree 1 holds for every program that can be written — the 400 sampled were a check on the implementation, never the grounds for the claim.

**Measured.** random_programs: 400; lengths: 1 to 12 gates; with_in_degree_1_everywhere: 400; percent: 100; worst_max_in_degree: 1; worst_unreachable: 0

**Note.** Four hundred random programs of random length, and every one has in-degree exactly 1 at all 27 states with zero unreachable. A composition of bijections is a bijection, so THERE IS NOTHING A PROGRAMMER CAN WRITE IN THIS LANGUAGE THAT BREAKS IT. Compare what factor four cost everywhere else: AI4 had to search 19,683 tables to find the 216 that work, and AJ1 needed the map to be built out of addition on purpose. Here it costs no analysis, no search and no discipline -- it is a property of the alphabet rather than of the program.

### `AK3` — HELD · NOT AT RISK

**Claim.** a straight-line reversible program costs its own length for every input, so the cost spread is exactly 1.00 and factor three is lost

**Not at risk.** Cost is defined as gate count and the language has no branching, so a straight-line program's spread of exactly 1.00 restates the cost model.

**Measured.** programs_measured: 50; largest_spread: 1; every_program_flat: true; AH1_three_word_spread: 513.8; countdown_spread: 25.38; threeway_spread: 1.02

**Note.** Every one of fifty straight-line programs costs exactly its own length in gates, for all 27 starting states: a spread of 1.0000. That is FLATTER THAN THE 1.02x AG1 CALLED SECURITY THEATRE, and against the 513.8x AH1 needed. Nothing in the language depends on the data, because branching on data means testing data and a test that discards its answer is erasing. So going fully reversible BUYS FACTOR FOUR AND LOSES FACTOR THREE, and the alternative registered -- that some program would show a spread above 1.00 and the worry was unfounded -- did not occur on any of them.

### `AK4` — HELD

**Claim.** a trilemma: in-degree one, a cost that varies, and bounded state are available two at a time and never three

**Measured.** constructions_tabulated: 6; with_all_three: 0; reversible_language: in-degree 1 + bounded state, cost flat; hailstone_and_three_word: cost varies + bounded state, in-degree above 1; reversible_plus_data_dependent: in-degree 1 + cost varies, state unbounded; history_growth: at least one trit per data-dependent step; thousand_steps_costs: 167 trytes of history

**Note.** Six constructions from this corpus tabulated against the three properties, and NONE HAS ALL THREE. The reversible language has in-degree one and bounded state with a flat cost; hailstone and the three-word program have a varying cost and bounded state with trajectories that merge; and buying the first two together is Bennett's construction -- a reversible machine CAN branch on data, but only by keeping the record of which way it went, so the history grows at least one trit per branch. A thousand data-dependent steps costs 167 trytes that can never be discarded, and AJ4 already measured what happens when bounded memory meets a state that will not stop growing: it wraps at term fifteen. IN-DEGREE ONE, A COST THAT VARIES, BOUNDED STATE -- PICK TWO.

So the phenomenon reproduces on a family that is NOT modular arithmetic, and whose hidden structure is a base-three FACTORISATION rather than a Fourier basis: the network sees a and b as opaque tokens in 0..26 and has to discover that the operation is positionwise in base three.

### `AM2` — FAILED

**Claim.** the affine task groks soonest, so the algebraic label predicts the outcome

**Measured.** affine_test90_by_seed: 7200, 10800, 16400, 10600, never; nonaffine_test90_by_seed: 3800, 8200, 6800, 5400, 6200; affine_median: 10800; nonaffine_median: 6200; nonaffine_faster_in: 4 of 4 paired seeds; affine_failed_to_generalise: 1 of 5 seeds within 40,000 steps; nonaffine_failed: 0 of 5; seeds: 5; identical: architecture, optimiser, split, step budget

**Note.** FAILED, and it inverted rather than merely missing. The AFFINE task -- ternary modular addition, which is what the grokking literature studies almost exclusively -- is the SLOWER of the two on every paired seed, with a median of 10,800 steps against 6,200, and on one seed it never reached 90% at all inside a 40,000-step budget while the non-affine task generalised on all five. Run once this would be a draw; run five times with everything but the algebra held fixed it is a direction. THE CANONICAL GROKKING TASK IS HARDER THAN A NON-AFFINE SIBLING, which is a comparison the literature has not been able to make because it has no labelled task ladder to make it on. Stated limit: one table per quadrant, so this measures seed-stability and not table-stability, and sweeping tables within a quadrant is the obvious next thing.

### `AM3` — FAILED

**Claim.** the erasing tasks have a majority-class baseline above 40% while the reversible ones sit near 3.7%

**Measured.** affine_erasing_baseline: 0.0457; nonaffine_erasing_baseline: 0.1918; affine_reversible_baseline: 0.0457; nonaffine_reversible_baseline: 0.0479; predicted_over: 0.4

**Note.** FAILED, and the reasoning behind it was the error. I conflated "erases in the leading argument" with "has a skewed output distribution", and they are different properties. The affine-erasing table is f = b, which is a BIJECTION in its second argument, so its outputs are perfectly uniform and its baseline is 0.0457 -- identical to the reversible tasks. Only tritwise MIN is genuinely skewed, at 0.1918, and even that is far short of 40%. AL3 had already shown the erasure column for that quadrant spans 1.585 to 3.170 and the table chosen sat at the uniform end, so the information needed to avoid this was on the record before the prediction was written.

### `AM4` — HELD

**Claim.** the affine-erasing quadrant is degenerate and is learned within a tenth of the steps the affine-reversible task needs

**Measured.** affine_erasing_test90: 200; affine_reversible_test90: 7200; ratio: 0.028; predicted_under: 0.1; affine_erasing_gap: 1; seconds: 4.4; tables_in_quadrant: 9; alpha_forced_zero: true

**Note.** Held at 0.028 against a predicted tenth: 200 steps versus 7,200, with no memorisation-to-generalisation gap at all. And it is degenerate BY PROOF rather than by luck -- an affine table is reversible in its leading argument exactly when alpha is nonzero, so affine AND erasing forces alpha = 0 and the function ignores its first input entirely. All nine tables in that quadrant are one-input functions, so the prediction covers the quadrant and not just the table trained.

## Set `AN` — Does a purpose-built search puzzle have the find-against-verify asymmetry? A ternary proof-of-work candidate, exhaustive over all 531,441 message-nonce pairs

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 3 held, 1 failed |
| tool | `tools/puzzle-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-puzzle.js` |
| registered | `a05b48e` |
| results | `32dfca9` |

### `AN1` — FAILED

**Claim.** the variance of hit counts across messages separates a compressing puzzle from a relabelling, landing within 25% of binomial at every difficulty while a bijective candidate gives exactly zero

**Measured.** arena: 729 messages x 729 nonces, 6-trit digest, exhaustive; feedforward_sd_over_binomial: 0.729, 0.674, 0.912, 0.871, 1.023, 0.994; registered_band: 0.75 to 1.25 at every k; failed_at: k = 1 and k = 2, both LOW; held_at: k = 3, 4, 5, 6; feedforward_mean_first_hit: 3.2, 9.1, 25.3, 81.0, 214.8, 311.2; null_mean_first_hit: 3.0, 9.0, 27.0, 80.9, 205.1, 305.2; first_hit_within: 15% at every k, as registered; bijective_sd: 0 at every k; affine_sd: 0 at every k; pseudorandom_control_sd_over_binomial: 0.973, 1.021, 1.051, 0.977, 1.023, 1.020

**Note.** FAILED at two of six difficulties, and the failure is the whole result. Two of the three legs held: the mean first hit sat within 15% of the finite-population null at every k, and both bijective controls gave a hit-count variance of EXACTLY zero against a binomial 12.73 -- which is the discriminator D4 could not supply, since truncating any permutation gives perfectly uniform buckets and a collision count therefore cannot separate a hash from a relabelling. The leg that failed is the one that mattered. The candidate came in at 0.729x and 0.674x of binomial at k = 1 and k = 2, MORE uniform than chance, and a puzzle more uniform than chance is structured. Chasing that deviation found the structure (see F-MESSAGE-COMMUTES-OUT-OF-A-GROUP-FEEDFORWARD). The registration said in advance that agreement would not be a certificate and that only disagreement could refute; the disagreement arrived and did exactly that.

### `AN2` — HELD

**Claim.** the tabulator kills a bijective puzzle and the algebra kills an affine one, both at one operation per solve, with affine strictly worse because it needs no table

**Measured.** tabulator_solved: 729/729 at every k from 1 to 6; tabulator_ops_per_solve: 1; tabulator_precompute: 729 entries; affine_solved: 729/729 at every k from 1 to 6; affine_ops_per_solve: 1; affine_precompute: 1 inversion of a 6x6 GF(3) matrix; brute_force_mean_attempts: 3.0, 9.0, 27.0, 80.9, 205.1, 305.2; speedup_at_k5: 205x, above the 180x registered; break_even_queries: 1; AD2_break_even_queries: 70

**Note.** Held on every clause. AD2 tabulated a program to price it and broke even at seventy queries; here the same attack breaks a bijective puzzle outright at one lookup, because a permutation can be walked backwards from the target. The affine candidate is strictly worse: the nonce is a rotation of a difference, so there is nothing to precompute but a single 6x6 inversion and the attack is profitable on query one. The gap between the two is exactly the 729-entry table. So the two algebraic labels this project has carried since AL are, for a puzzle, both disqualifying -- and in a strict order.

### `AN3` — HELD

**Claim.** a puzzle that is non-invertible in the nonce strands messages at the null rate, and a bijective one strands none

**Measured.** feedforward_stranded: 0, 0, 0, 0, 33, 264; null_stranded: 0.000, 0.000, 0.000, 0.085, 36.071, 268.000; within_factor_of_two_at: k = 5 and k = 6; monotone_in_k: true; bijective_stranded: 0 at every k; affine_stranded: 0 at every k; fraction_unmineable_at_max_difficulty: 36.2%; survives_the_keyed_fix: 35 and 283 at k = 5 and k = 6

**Note.** Held, and it is the symmetric twin of the receipt result. The receipt died needing in-degree one; the puzzle NEEDS in-degree above one, or AN2(a) inverts it -- and pays for that in messages no nonce can mine. At maximum difficulty 264 of 729 messages, 36.2%, have no solution at all, and a miner holding one grinds forever. Both bijective controls strand exactly zero, so the property that guarantees every message is mineable is the same property that lets an attacker skip the mining. The number survives the keyed reconstruction (35 and 283), which is what shows the result is about compression rather than about this particular construction.

### `AN4` — HELD

**Claim.** widening the nonce cures the stranding and the understated work at once, because both are one symptom of the nonce space failing to outrun the target rarity

**Measured.** narrow_nonce: 729; narrow_stranded_at_k6: 264; narrow_mean_first_hit: 311.2; wide_nonce: 531441; wide_stranded_at_k6: 0; wide_mean_first_hit: 735; target_3_to_the_k: 729; within: 0.8% of 3^6, against a registered 10%; truncated_understatement: 58%

**Note.** Held on both halves, and they moved together. A twelve-trit nonce absorbed in two blocks through the same compression function strands nothing at maximum difficulty and raises the mean search from 311.2 to 735.0, which is within 0.8% of 3^6 = 729 -- the figure a proper lottery owes and the one a truncated nonce space understates by 58%. So AN3 is not a fact about irreversibility as such but about a nonce space too small for the target, and the design rule is measured rather than borrowed: nonce space must exceed target rarity by orders of magnitude. That is what the extraNonce field in Bitcoin is for.

## Set `AO` — Can an erasing machine certify that a secret was wiped? Ceremony maps over 729 secrets, and whether the erasure measure is the right certificate

| | |
|---|---|
| outcome | 3 held, 1 failed |
| tool | `tools/wipe-audit.js` |
| asserted in | `test/test-wipe.js` |
| registered | `068a161` |
| results | `fdef33a` |

### `AO1` — FAILED

**Claim.** the pseudorandom ceremony map measures E within 5% of the 0.8265 null while exposing, within 10% of 268, secrets whose preimage is a single point

**Measured.** E: 0.8894; E_null: 0.8265; E_deviation: 7.6%, against a registered 5%; secrets_fully_exposed: 252; exposed_null: 268.4; exposed_deviation: 6.1%, inside the registered 10%; fraction_exposed: 34.6%; smallest_preimage: 1; image: 446; outputs_never_produced: 283; control_draw_position: 2.09 sd from the mean of 400 draws; draws_that_would_pass_the_5pc_band: 336 of 400

**Note.** FAILED on the erasure clause and held on the one that carried the argument, and the post-mortem is worth more than either. E came in at 0.8894 against a null of 0.8265 -- 7.6% out where 5% was registered. Sweeping 400 pseudorandom maps then showed the null was exactly right (mean 0.8269, sd 0.0299) and that 336 of 400 draws WOULD have passed the 5% band. The band was reasonable; the draw was not. This set fixed one seed as its control and happened to fix a 2.09-sigma one, so the failure is about the sample and not about the criterion or the claim. A SINGLE FIXED PSEUDORANDOM MAP CANNOT BE SCORED AGAINST A DISTRIBUTIONAL NULL: it is one sample and the null is a spread. The exposed clause survived on the same unlucky draw only because it was given a 10% band rather than a 5% one. And the substance held completely: 252 of 729 secrets, 34.6%, are recovered EXACTLY from the public output while the average erasure reads healthy at 0.89 bits. E is a mean and hiding is a minimum.

### `AO2` — HELD · PROVEN

**Claim.** truncating the mixer to m trits gives every output exactly 3^(6-m) preimages, minimum equal to maximum, while the pseudorandom map has a minimum of 1

**Argument.** The mixer is a bijection, so the 729 secrets land on 729 distinct values; grouping those by their low m trits partitions them into 3^m classes of exactly 3^(6-m). Flatness is forced by the pigeonhole equality, not observed -- and it holds at every width where the truncation divides the space.

**Measured.** m1: {"image":3,"min":243,"max":243,"E":7.9248}; m3: {"image":27,"min":27,"max":27,"E":4.7549}; m5: {"image":243,"min":3,"max":3,"E":1.585}; flat_at_every_m: true; random_min: 1; random_max: 6; random_flat: false

**Note.** Held exactly at every m from 1 to 5. The point is the reuse: D4 FAILED because truncating any permutation gives perfectly uniform buckets, which made a collision count useless as evidence of mixing. That same forced uniformity is precisely what a wipe wants -- every secret hidden among exactly as many others as every other secret, with no output easier to invert than another. A construction disqualified as a hash test is the right answer to a different question, and the disqualifying property IS the qualifying one.

### `AO3` — HELD

**Claim.** truncation attains the pigeonhole hiding bound at every power of three and the pseudorandom map attains it nowhere

**Measured.** bound: image <= floor(729/h); bits_at_h_1_3_9_27: [9.5098,7.9248,6.3399,4.7549]; truncation_attains: h = 1, 3, 9, 27 — all four; random_attains: none; flat_maps_among_400_random_draws: 0

**Note.** Held on both clauses. The bound itself is arithmetic -- every preimage of at least h forces an image of at most floor(729/h) -- so what was at risk was attainment, and the split is total: truncation attains it at all four, the pseudorandom map at none, and not one of 400 random draws is even flat. A balanced wipe does not happen by accident. The exchange rate is the useful number: to hide every secret among 27 others the public output may carry 4.755 of its 9.510 bits, so HIDING IS BOUGHT WITH OUTPUT BITS at a fixed price, and a ceremony whose parameters must be large enough to be useful cannot buy much of it.

### `AO4` — HELD

**Claim.** the count of fully-exposed secrets lands within 10% of both the 268 null and AN3's measured 264 stranded blocks, because both are tails of the same Poisson(1)

**Measured.** exposed: 252; null: 268.4; AN3_stranded: 264; deviation_from_null: 6.1%; deviation_from_AN3: 4.5%; reason: P(Poisson(1)=0) = P(Poisson(1)=1) = 1/e, so the two tails are equal by construction; this_map_unused_outputs: 283

**Note.** Held on both comparisons. A block with no winning nonce and a secret with a unique preimage are the k=0 and k=1 tails of the same Poisson(1), and Poisson(1) puts identical mass on those two, so the counts are equal by construction rather than by coincidence. AN3 measured 264 unmineable blocks; AO measures 252 unhidden secrets; the shared null is 268. Two results this project reached by different routes, four sets apart, are the same number, and neither set knew it.

### `AP1` — HELD

**Claim.** an attacker holding one valid signature can forge exactly one message, the one already signed

**Measured.** signed_messages_swept: 729; targets_per_message: 729; worst_case_forgeable: 1; messages_admitting_a_second: 0; control_no_signature: 0 of 729; control_all_signatures: 729 of 729

**Note.** Held exhaustively. Every one of the 729 signed messages forges exactly itself and nothing else, so the scheme is not broken at first use -- which is the assumption everything else in the set rests on. The controls pin both ends of the meter: holding no signature forges nothing, holding all of them forges everything.

### `AP2` — HELD

**Claim.** two signatures under one key leak at the binomial rate, mean within 5% of 21.43, maximum 64 and minimum 1

**Measured.** ordered_pairs: 531441; mean_forgeable: 21.433; null: 21.43; agreement: 0.01%; maximum: 64; maximum_is: 2^6, when the messages differ in all six positions; minimum: 1; minimum_is: signing the same message twice, which reveals nothing new; mean_share: 2.94%; worst_share: 8.78%

**Note.** Held on all three clauses, and the mean agrees with the closed form to one part in ten thousand -- which is the real content, because it confirms the binomial model is the right description of what a reused key gives away rather than merely a plausible one. The one-time restriction is therefore not advisory: a second signature under the same key hands away 2.94% of the message space on average and 8.78% at worst, and there is no configuration in which it hands away nothing unless the same message is signed twice.

### `AP3` — HELD · NOT AT RISK

**Claim.** ternary leaks less of its own space than binary on key reuse, 2.94% against 5.63%

**Not at risk.** The project's own verdict at the time, already recorded in the note and in should_not_have_been_registered: both sides are the closed form (1 + (b-1)/b)^pos and the registration computed both before the run.

**Measured.** ternary: 2.94% of 729; binary: 5.63% of 1024; ratio: 1.92; registered_ratio: 1.91; mechanism: trits differ with p = 2/3 against bits at 1/2, so the per-position rate is HIGHER for ternary and the leak is still lower, because the position count falls faster; should_not_have_been_registered: true

**Note.** Held, including the mechanism clause -- ternary digits collide more often and leak less anyway, because six positions against ten outweighs two thirds against one half. But it should not have been registered. Both sides are the closed form (1 + (b-1)/b)^pos and the registration itself computed both before the run, so nothing here was ever at risk. AGENTS.md names this failure directly: inflating the registered set with facts that were never at risk turns the discipline into decoration. Recorded as held and as a registration that should not have been made.

### `AP4` — HELD · NOT AT RISK

**Claim.** ternary pays for that advantage in destruction: 12 of 18 preimages against 10 of 20, and strictly more erased bits

**Not at risk.** The project's own verdict at the time, already recorded in the note and in should_not_have_been_registered: (b-1)/b and the projection erasure are closed forms over a scheme whose base and position count the registration stipulated.

**Measured.** ternary: 18 preimages, 6 revealed, 12 destroyed, 66.7%; binary: 20 preimages, 10 revealed, 10 destroyed, 50.0%; erasure_per_position: ternary 3.1699 bits, binary 1.5850; erasure_total: ternary 19.020 bits, binary 15.850; should_not_have_been_registered: true

**Note.** Held. The wipe is a projection from a b-tuple of preimages onto the one revealed, and AB's own erasure measure agrees with the closed form log2(ALPHA^(b-1)) exactly, so the ternary key destroys 19.020 bits of material against binary's 15.850. AP3's leak advantage is bought with a larger wipe, and AO already priced what a wipe costs. Like AP3 this was arithmetic before it was measured: (b-1)/b and the projection erasure are both closed forms, and the only thing genuinely measured was that erasureOf agrees with them.

## Set `AQ` — How wide should an authenticated tree be, and does a power of three ever beat a power of two? A cost model over every integer branching factor from 2 to 1024, 45 leaf counts, and a bytes-per-verify-operation exchange rate swept across eight decades

### `AQ1` — FAILED

**Claim.** binary is never optimal for a vector commitment, the optimum never descends past three, and across the swept leaf counts THREE is the large-gamma optimum more often than four

**At risk.** the first half leans on a continuous argument and this set exists because ceilings break those. depth(N, 2) can fall well below the smooth law at particular N, and one cell with argmin 2 refutes it. The second half -- which of 3 and 4 wins more leaf counts -- I cannot call at all.

**Measured.** cells: 2880; cells_with_argmin_two: 0; narrowest_optimum: 3; widest_optimum: 1024; distinct_optima: 61; cells_where_optimum_widens_as_verify_dearer: 0; leaf_counts_preferring_three_at_the_limit: 21; leaf_counts_preferring_four_at_the_limit: 21

**Note.** Failed on its last clause, and that clause was the whole point. The first three parts held exactly: no cell in 2,880 has argmin 2, the optimum never goes below 3, and it never widens as verifying gets dearer. But three does not beat four at the verify-dominated limit -- it TIES, 21 leaf counts each. Chasing the tie produced F-TREE-BRANCHES-IN-ITS-OWN-BASE, which is a better answer than the one predicted: 3^k leaf counts want three and 2^k leaf counts want four, so the tie was a property of how many of each shape this sweep contains rather than of trees. T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN, fourth bite. NARROWED AFTERWARDS, AND STATED HERE SO A READER OF AQ ALONE IS NOT MISLED: AR4 lifted the constant-arity constraint every tree in this sweep was built under, and F-TREE-BRANCHES-IN-ITS-OWN-BASE turned out to be a property of CONSTANT trees rather than of trees. 25 of these 45 leaf counts change shape once radix sequences are admitted, 11 of the 18 powers of three among them, and N = 729 wants [4,4,4,4,3] rather than six threes -- for 0.0178% of the total cost, a surface flat to four decimal places. AR's evidence for that is FREQUENCY and not magnitude: its null over 100 redraws has a tail reaching 23.7%, ABOVE the subject's own worst cell, so a structureless per-level cost can produce a larger maximum than the real regime does, while the frequency of improvement separates a hundredfold. T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN, fifth bite, and the second time the class has bitten this same sentence.

### `AQ2` — FAILED

**At risk.** entirely, and the arithmetic starts against it. Ten powers of two sit in 2..1024 and only six powers of three, so the geometry has to overcome a handicap of almost two to one.

But PER ARITY IN RANGE the ordering reverses -- each power of three wins 137 cells against each power of two's 104 -- so the registered wording measured how many of each arity I put in the sweep as much as it measured the trees. The claim was answerable only because a design decision had already half-decided it.

### `AQ3` — HELD

**At risk.** AT RISK, and deliberately against the obvious answer: a unit is a scale factor and a scale factor cannot move an argmin. The escape is that a proof travels in whole units, so rounding each term up reintroduces a ceiling, and near-ties between adjacent arities are common enough that one should flip. If this fails, the unit is free and that is worth knowing too.

**Measured.** argmins_moved: 8; cells: 2880; fraction: 0.0028; argmins_moved_under_the_registered_conversion: 103

Caught before scoring because a 19% unit change cannot honestly move an optimum from three to six. T-INSTRUMENT-FALSE-VERDICT, eighteenth bite. The wrong conversion is kept in the tool and both numbers are pinned, so the fix cannot silently regress.

### `AQ4` — FAILED

**Claim.** at every cell where either arity is within 15% of that cell's optimum, the totals at branching factor 64 and 256 differ by no more than 15%

**Measured.** cells_where_either_is_near_optimal: 909; cells_exceeding_the_fifteen_percent_band: 571; worst_spread_percent: 148.8; of_those_at_different_depths: 426; of_those_at_the_same_depth: 145

**Note.** Failed and not narrowly -- 571 of 909, worst case 149%. But 426 of those 571 are cells where 64 and 256 sit at DIFFERENT DEPTHS, and when 256 saves a whole level it wins by that level while when it does not it pays four times the verify for nothing. So the two are close to interchangeable at a fixed depth and completely different across a depth step, which makes the answer a fact about the leaf count rather than about either arity. The question as asked -- is 64 as good as 256 -- has no answer that does not name N.

### `AR3` — HELD

**Claim.** variation helps most leaf counts, not a few: over the deep contiguous window at the verify-dominated rate, more than half of the leaf counts have a strictly cheaper varying optimum

**At risk.** AT RISK, AND THIS IS THE ONE I CANNOT CALL: it comes out the other way if the constant optimiser's freedom to pick its own depth is worth as much as the sequence's freedom to pick its own widths, and I have no way to settle that short of running it. The reasoning FOR is that a constant tree must round every level up together while a sequence rounds only a minority of them, so equality needs the rounding remainder to land on 0 or on d, roughly a 2/(d+1) coincidence. The evidence AGAINST is my own: of six leaf counts I worked by hand, four were NOT helped. I am registering the reasoning against my own sample, which is the choice that can embarrass me, and if the sample is right rather than the reasoning then the flexibility is a rarity rather than a rule and `AR1`'s bound describes a corner case.

**Measured.** leaf_counts: 7169; helped: 6144; helped_percent: 85.7; unhelped: 1025; optima_that_are_a_constant_arity: 1025; null_helped_percent: 0.83

**Note.** Held, and it is the one the registration said could not be called. 6,144 of 7,169 leaf counts -- 85.7% -- have a strictly cheaper varying optimum, against a null of 0.83% of draw-by-leaf pairs: a hundredfold separation, and the statistic that actually shows the effect is structure rather than arithmetic. I registered the reasoning against my own hand sample and the reasoning was right; the sample was drawn at powers, which is where a constant tree is at its best. The unhelped 1,025 are EXACTLY the leaf counts whose optimal tree is a constant arity, with no exceptions in 7,169 -- and those are powers of FOUR rather than powers in general, since four is the arity the optimum wants. 2187 = 3^7 is helped.

### `AR4` — FAILED

**Claim.** the optimal tree gets deeper more often than shallower: over the deep contiguous window at the verify-dominated rate, leaf counts whose varying optimum is strictly deeper than their constant optimum outnumber those whose varying optimum is strictly shallower

**At risk.** it comes out the other way if the per-level bytes charge O outweighs the per-level rounding slack, and I have a worked case where it does -- at N = 10^8 the hand arithmetic puts the varying optimum THREE levels SHALLOWER than the constant one, which is the direction opposite to the one registered. Both declared tie-breaks also push against it: the constant baseline breaks ties toward the smaller arity and so toward the deeper tree, and the sequence breaks ties toward the smaller depth and so toward the shallower one. The reasoning FOR is only that the slack a sequence exploits is per-level, so there is more of it where there are more levels.

**Measured.** leaf_counts: 7169; deeper: 2176; shallower: 3580; same_depth: 1413; ratio_shallower_to_deeper: 1.65; verify_budget_identical: 2861; verify_budget_smaller: 4308; verify_budget_larger: 0; shallower_at_identical_verify_budget: 1836

**Note.** FAILED, and inverted rather than narrowly missed: 3,580 shallower against 2,176 deeper, 1.6 to 1. The registered reasoning had the mechanism backwards. It argued that more levels means more per-level slack to exploit, so the tree should grow. What a sequence actually buys is the SAME verify budget in FEWER levels: the quantity gamma is charged on is never larger than the constant tree's, it is identical at 2,861 of 7,169 leaf counts, and 1,836 of the 3,580 shallower cells are of exactly that kind. THE SLACK REMOVES A LEVEL RATHER THAN ADDING ONE, and the saving there is level overhead rather than work. That mechanism is what overturns AQ's headline: 25 of AQ's 45 leaf counts change shape, 11 of the 18 powers of three among them, and N = 729 wants [4,4,4,4,3] rather than six threes -- for 0.0178% of the total cost.

The same structure with a LINEAR round function gives 92 cycles and order 8, so the structure is not what mixes: the round function's nonlinearity is.

The state with L = R and round(R) = 0 is fixed; the round table is a permutation, so exactly one R maps to 0. That is a structural fingerprint rather than a statistic, and a fixed point is an input that no number of rounds ever moves. The standard remedy is a per-round CONSTANT, which collides with the one-function-called-repeatedly rule unless the round counter is carried inside the state.

- **`F-BORN-NONLINEAR`** — The design intuition inverts between the two bases. Neither reading is wrong; the boundary is a modelling choice that must be declared before any number means anything.

Swept over all 729 inputs, 3n+1 terminates on exactly six of them -- the powers of three. Replacing the climb with 2n + low_trit mixes the residue and terminates on 363. Measured while choosing the rule, not predicted.

More things to say, far less structure to say them with.

Nobody predicted this; AF1 only asked about individual intervals.

- **`F-WIDTH-AND-VARIANCE-ARE-INDEPENDENT`** — A program can have a wide live state and a nearly constant cost, or a narrow state and a wide cost range, and the two do not track each other. threeway has five live input words and a cost spread of 1.02x; countdown has one live word and a spread of 25.38x. So an implied receipt rests on THREE factors and not two: reachable state count, cost per evaluation, and the variance of the cost itself -- and if the third is near zero the other two do not matter, because a predictor guesses the commonest answer instead of tabulating.

The three-word program has a control space of 387 million against hailstone's 729 -- five hundred thousand times larger -- and still reuses each visited state 3.20 times against hailstone's 10.43. A subtractive inner loop converges onto shared suffixes whenever two inputs agree on the subtrahend, whatever their starting values. So an implied receipt rests on FOUR things and not three: state count, cost per evaluation, cost variance, and how tree-like the trajectory graph is.
  <br>*Evidence:* AH2, 120 inputs against hailstone's 729, both on one reuse instrument
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-margin.js`

AI4 predicted a quarter unreachable and a maximum in-degree of three; the real figures are far more extreme, which means a collapsing feedback is not a weak receipt but a state space that mostly does not exist.
  <br>*Evidence:* AI4, exhaustive in-degree census over all 531,441 states of the two-input shift register
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-arity.js`
- **`F-SELF-REFERENCE-IS-NOT-THE-PROPERTY`** — The history operator gives a tabulator-proof trajectory graph, and self-reference is not why. Its step map is injective because it is built entirely out of addition, which erases nothing -- so a forgetful two-word carry has the property as fully as an append-only history. Self-reference in the strong sense is separately unavailable by the Ladder's own Coda III, which proves no system closes over its own semantics and shows that two of the three verdicts of nf(t) are not in the term. What was being asked for is reversibility, and it is cheaper than what was being proposed.
  <br>*Evidence:* AJ1 exhaustive over 531,441 states, AB2's measurement of ADD at zero bits, and Coda III of the external Ladder artifact
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-selfref.js`
- **`F-REVERSIBILITY-IS-A-PROPERTY-OF-THE-ALPHABET`** — Where factor four is bought decides what it costs to keep. AI4 bought it by searching 19,683 tables for the 216 that work, and AJ1 by building a map deliberately out of addition -- both are properties of a particular program that a later edit could destroy. Choosing a reversible ALPHABET makes it a property of the language: 400 of 400 random programs have it, and no program can be written that does not. The same guarantee, at three different prices, and only the last one survives a programmer.
  <br>*Evidence:* AK2 against AI4 and AJ1, all three measured on in-degree over their own state spaces
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-minimal.js`
- **`F-CANONICAL-GROKKING-TASK-IS-THE-HARD-ONE`** — Ternary modular addition -- the affine task, and the family the grokking literature studies almost exclusively -- generalises more slowly than a non-affine reversible sibling under a controlled comparison holding architecture, optimiser, split, seed and step budget fixed. Median 10,800 steps against 6,200, slower on 4 of 4 paired seeds, and on a fifth it failed to reach 90% inside 40,000 steps while the non-affine task succeeded on all five. Nobody predicted this; AM2 predicted the opposite.
  <br>*Evidence:* AM2, five seeds per task on an NVIDIA GB10, 729-pair arena at 40% train
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-grok.js`
- **`F-MESSAGE-COMMUTES-OUT-OF-A-GROUP-FEEDFORWARD`** — A Davies-Meyer feed-forward whose message enters the data path through the SAME group operation as the nonce is not a puzzle at all. h(m,n) = P(m + n) - n collapses identically to g(m + n) + m with g(u) = P(u) - u, verified on all 531,441 pairs, so every message is one puzzle shifted. One 729-entry inverted index of g then solves every mineable message in 1.54 lookups against a brute force of 3.0 to 305.2, and correctly declares the rest unmineable rather than failing on them. Keying the permutation with the message instead -- true Davies-Meyer -- destroys the identity and returns the hit-count variance to within 3% of binomial at every difficulty. A fix that removes the symptom is what confirms the cause.
  <br>*Evidence:* AN1 failing LOW at k = 1 and k = 2 was the only signal; tools/puzzle-audit.js, exhaustive at 729 states
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-puzzle.js`
- **`F-STRANDING-IS-AN-IMAGE-DEFICIT`** — The stranded messages and the shortcut are one object, not two findings. g(u) = P(u) - u has an image of 465 of 729 digests, and 729 - 465 = 264 is EXACTLY the number of messages AN3 counted as unmineable at maximum difficulty. A message is mineable at the tightest target precisely when its shifted target lies in that image, so the size of the image is the mining participation rate. Nothing predicted the two numbers would be the same number.
  <br>*Evidence:* AN3 and the post-registration section of tools/puzzle-audit.js
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-puzzle.js`
- **`F-AFFINE-HIDES-ITS-SOLUTIONS-FROM-A-SCAN`** — An affine puzzle gives every message exactly the right NUMBER of solutions and puts them in the wrong PLACES. At k = 3 every message has exactly 27 valid nonces, as a bijection must, yet a sequential scan needs 248 attempts to reach one where the null says 27 -- so the honest miner does nine times the expected work while the algebraic attack does one operation. The gap between honest and attacker is therefore wider than AN2 measured, and a hit COUNT alone would have missed it.
  <br>*Evidence:* AN1 first-hit column for the affine candidate: 4.0, 5.0, 248.0, 329.0, 356.0, 365.0
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-puzzle.js`
- **`F-REVERSIBLE-CANNOT-DESTROY`** · PROVEN — A machine built from AK's language cannot destroy a secret, so it cannot run a trusted-setup ceremony. Injectivity is closed under composition (AK2), so no program maps two distinct starting states to the same final state: two different secrets stay distinguishable for ever, and every intermediate state determines the initial one. Erasure, as this project defines it, is exactly the collapse that cannot occur — so the ceremony's "and then delete s" step is not merely unperformed but INEXPRESSIBLE in the language. The property AK was built to guarantee is the property that forbids it.
  <br>*Argument:* Corollary of AK2 and the definition of erasure. E = 0 for every program in a language all of whose primitives are bijections, and a secret is destroyed only when the final state is constant in it — which requires E > 0.
  <br>*Evidence:* AK2, and the erasure measure defined in AB; checked in test/test-minimal.js
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-minimal.js`
- **`F-LAMPORT-BASE-ADVANTAGE-IS-NOT-PER-SIZE`** · PROVEN — A Lamport key costs b preimages per position and log_b N positions, so b / ln b per value -- minimised at b = e, which puts three ahead of two by 5.4% asymptotically. That advantage does NOT hold at every width, because the position count is an integer: sweeping ten digest sizes, binary wins at 256 and 1024, the two tie at 64 and 4096, and ternary takes the other six. An asymptotic argument does not settle a particular width.
  <br>*Argument:* Cost per value is b * log_b N / log N = b / ln b, whose derivative vanishes at b = e; 3/ln3 = 2.731 against 2/ln2 = 2.885. The per-size flip follows from ceil(log_b N) being a step function: at N = 2^k the binary position count is exact while the ternary one rounds up.
  <br>*Evidence:* measured while choosing the arena for AP, which is exactly when a fact stops being a prediction
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-keylayer.js`
- **`F-FINDABILITY-NOT-COUNT`** — A summed ledger head and a hashed one carry the same 9.5098 bits about a history of any length, so a collision COUNT cannot separate them. What separates them is findability. Over one six-entry ledger, all 21,840 compensating pairs -- add d to one entry, subtract it from another, leave the total alone -- were accepted by the summed head, every single one, and 26 were accepted by the split-round mixer fed forward, against a chance rate of 29.96. The control says the compensating structure is doing the work: of the 4,368 single edits, which move the total, the summed head accepted 0 and the mixer accepted 7 against a chance rate of 6.
  <br>*Argument:* The summed head is linear in the entries, so a compensating pair is not a search at all -- it is one equation with a solution by construction. The mixer chain a' = P(a + e) - e has no such solution, so a forger is reduced to trying, and 26 of 21,840 is what trying gets.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/ledger-audit.js sweeps both accumulators over the same 21,840 forgeries and the same 4,368 single-edit controls
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-ledger.js`
- **`F-MIXER-HEAD-IS-NOT-FLAT`** — The N^(L-1) collision count is a property of an IDEAL hash, and the concrete mixer is not one. Over all 531,441 two-entry ledgers the summed head is exactly flat at 729 preimages per head, while the split-round chain ranges from 629 to 851 -- 17 percent above the ideal at its peak. No head is unreachable, so the chain is onto and the bias is in the spread rather than in the range.
  <br>*Argument:* The summed head is flat because addition is a bijection in the last entry, which fixes the preimage count at N^(L-1) by construction. The chain step P(a + e) - e is NOT a bijection in e -- that non-invertibility is exactly what AN registered it for -- so its preimage counts are free to vary, and they do.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/ledger-audit.js preimageProfile(2), a full enumeration rather than a sample
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-ledger.js`
- **`F-TREE-BRANCHES-IN-ITS-OWN-BASE`** — Once verifying dominates bandwidth, an authenticated tree wants the branching factor its leaf count is written in. Of 18 leaf counts of the form 3^k, 15 take branching factor three; of 19 of the form 2^k, 13 take four. The two shapes are almost equally represented in the sweep, which is the entire reason AQ1 saw a 21-21 tie rather than a result. NARROWED BY SET AR, AND THE ORIGINAL WORDING IS KEPT ABOVE BECAUSE IT IS WHAT WAS FOUND: this holds only under the constraint that every level of the tree uses the SAME arity, which is the one constraint every tree in AQ's sweep was built under. Lift it and 25 of these 45 leaf counts change shape, 11 of the 18 powers of three among them -- N = 729 prefers the radix sequence [4,4,4,4,3] to six threes. It prefers it by 0.0178% of the total cost, so the surface this preference was read off is flat to four decimal places. A TREE BRANCHES IN ITS OWN BASE IS A PROPERTY OF CONSTANT TREES.
  <br>*Argument:* At large gamma the cost is dominated by depth times arity, and depth is ceil(log_b N). When N is an exact power of b the ceiling is tight and no level is wasted; when it is not, the top level is partly empty and paid for in full. A leaf count of 3^k therefore pays nothing for branching by three and rounds up for branching by four, and the reverse holds for 2^k.
  <br>*Scope:* The narrowing is AR4 and F-THE-ARITY-OPTIMUM-IS-FLAT, at 12b5570. What survives is the constant-arity statement, which is still true and still explains AQ1's 21-21 tie. What does not survive is the noun: the sweep visited one design -- trees of a single width -- and the sentence named trees. T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN, fifth bite, already counted at AR's results commit rather than here.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/branching-audit.js limitPreference(), over the 45 leaf counts of set AQ
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-branching.js`
- **`F-CONTROL-CANNOT-DISCRIMINATE`** · PROVEN — Set AQ's registered control could not have detected the failure it was written to detect. Its two cost terms are the same pseudorandom draw, so its total is d*NOISE[b]*(1+gamma) and gamma factors out entirely: its optimum is invariant in the exchange rate at every one of the 45 leaf counts. A post-hoc control drawing the two terms independently gives 7 distinct optima with 131 backward steps and a narrowest optimum of 207, against the vector regime's 61 optima, 0 backward steps and narrowest optimum of 3 -- which is what actually establishes that the vector regime is structure rather than the shape of the arithmetic.
  <br>*Argument:* A control exists to show that the instrument does not manufacture the effect. If the swept parameter cancels out of the control algebraically, the control is constant in exactly the dimension the claim is about, and it can only ever agree.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/branching-audit.js argminControl2() and control2Profile(); the invariance is checked exhaustively rather than argued
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-branching.js`
- **`F-RADIX-ORDER-IS-FREE`** · PROVEN — In this cost model a radix sequence's total depends on it only through its MULTISET of arities -- indeed only through the depth d and the sum of the arities. A tree that is three at the top and nine below costs exactly what nine at the top and three below costs. There is no schedule to choose, only a multiset.
  <br>*Argument:* Every regime charges a per-level weight and the weights add, so the total is sum over levels of w(b_i), which is symmetric in the levels. For the merkle and vector regimes w is affine in b, so the sum collapses further to a function of d and sum(b_i) alone. This is what makes the whole search reduce to MINSUM(d, N) and it is immediate from the construction rather than discovered.
  <br>*Scope:* An order-SENSITIVE cost -- a verifier caching the top levels, an update path charged differently from a read -- is a different model, and nothing in set AR bounds it.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/radix-audit.js costOfSequence(); [3,9,27] and [27,9,3] are asserted equal in both regimes at three exchange rates
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-radix.js`
- **`F-MERKLE-WANTS-BINARY-AT-EVERY-LEVEL`** · PROVEN — In the merkle regime, letting the arity vary buys exactly nothing at any leaf count and any exchange rate. The all-twos tree is optimal, and it is optimal by proof rather than by sweep.
  <br>*Argument:* Merkle cost is (H + gamma) * sum(b_i - 1). For every integer b >= 2, b - 1 >= log2(b) with equality only at b = 2, so sum(b_i - 1) >= log2(prod b_i) >= log2(N). The cost is an integer multiple of (H + gamma), and the all-twos tree attains ceil(log2 N), which is the least integer above that floor. No sequence can do better and only all-twos attains it.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/radix-audit.js bestSequence vs bestConstant in the merkle regime over all 2,880 grid cells, plus the inequality checked at every arity from 2 to 1024
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-radix.js`
- **`F-THE-ARITY-OPTIMUM-IS-FLAT`** — The cost surface over arity choices is nearly flat where AQ read a preference off it. Admitting radix sequences changes the SHAPE of the optimal tree at 25 of AQ's 45 leaf counts -- including 11 of the 18 powers of three, AQ's own headline case, where N = 729 wants [4,4,4,4,3] rather than six threes -- while changing the COST by 0.0133% to 0.0251% at the median, and 13 of the 25 shape changes are worth under 0.5%.
  <br>*Argument:* At those leaf counts the sequence achieves the SAME gamma-charged quantity d + sum(b_i) as AQ's constant tree and simply spends fewer levels reaching it, so the entire saving is per-level byte overhead. At N = 3^12 both cost 48 units of verify and the sequence uses ten levels where the constant tree uses twelve.
  <br>*Scope:* This says the arity line of a descriptor is under-determined BY THIS COST MODEL. A model with an order-sensitive or implementation-sensitive term could easily separate the candidates this one cannot.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/radix-audit.js limitShapes() over AQ's 45 leaf counts at the verify-dominated rate
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-radix.js`
- **`F-VARYING-HELPS-IFF-THE-OPTIMUM-IS-NOT-CONSTANT`** — A leaf count is helped by letting the arity vary EXACTLY when its own optimal tree is not a constant one. Over the 7,169 leaf counts of the deep window there are no exceptions: 1,025 are unhelped and the same 1,025 have a constant optimum. The unhelped counts are the powers of FOUR rather than powers in general, because four is the arity the optimum wants; 2187 = 3^7 is helped.
  <br>*Argument:* One direction is immediate -- if the optimal sequence is constant it is available to the constant optimiser, so nothing is gained. The other direction is not forced by anything in the construction and is what the measurement adds: no leaf count has a strictly non-constant optimum that merely ties the best constant tree.
  <br>*Evidence:* tools/radix-audit.js bestSequence and bestConstant over every integer leaf count in [1024, 8192] at the verify-dominated rate
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-radix.js`
- **`F-REGISTRATION-IS-NOT-RISK`** — Registering a prediction does not make it a prediction. A read-only audit of all 181 predictions registered as of 1acfeee scored 25 of them DECORATIVE -- the answer and its derivation both standing in the registration's own text, over quantities the registrant stipulated -- and 7 it could not call. PUBLISHED: 181 registered, 149 held, 32 failed, a 17.7% failure rate. CORRECTED to what was genuinely at risk: 149 registered, 117 held, 32 failed, 21.5%. Both numbers are true and they answer different questions, so both are kept and neither replaces the other; 181 predictions were registered and that is a fact about what happened. The failures were never the problem -- all 32 are real, and not one of them is among the 25, which is the rule validating itself, since a fact that was never at risk cannot fail. What is not evidence is 25 of the 149 successes.
  <br>*Argument:* The rule scored only what the registration itself wrote down, and it read that text with `git show <registered_at>:<tool>` rather than from the working tree, so no later editing of a docstring can move a verdict. Four routes to decorative: arithmetic performed inside the block; forcing by a theorem the block states; restatement of a definition or of a sibling's conclusion; and a commitment about the phase's own paperwork rather than about the machine. The 25 are spread across 18 of the 43 sets and the rate does not fall over time, so this is a habit rather than an early-project artefact. IT IS NOT THE SAME AXIS AS `basis`, which looks as though it should have caught it: only 5 of the 10 `proven` predictions are decorative, and 20 of the 25 decorative ones are marked `measured`. A derivation can be genuinely at risk because the derivation may be WRONG -- AK1's registration typed a group order at 25 digits where the true value has 28, and held only because the claim named the group rather than the numeral. AQ was the only one of the 43 sets audited that wrote `AT RISK` lines into its registration and the only one that scored zero decorative; AR, the 44th, was registered the same way. That is a sample of two, and two agents happening to have been told about it is not an antibody, which is why the annotation is now compulsory rather than advisory. Finally the count is a FLOOR: the rule cannot see arithmetic a registrant did silently, and six of the 25 -- Q4, R5, G1, AJ4, AE2, AL2 -- are contestable. Conceding all six leaves 19 and does not change the verdict.
  <br>*Evidence:* The `at_risk` field on every prediction in this manifest, parsed by `tools/at-risk.js`; the 25 and the 7 are frozen as literal lists in `test/test-findings.js` so they cannot be quietly unmarked, and the corrected rate is generated into the prose by `tools/render-docs.js` beside the raw counts rather than instead of them. A verdict may be moved, but only LOUDLY: the manifest's `reaudits` list is where a departure from that baseline is argued, and an id absent from it may not change bucket. Sticky rather than immovable — an immovable list would make the CORPUS wrong on the day somebody earned a change, and the only way green would be to leave a known-false annotation standing.
  <br>*Asserted in:* `test/test-findings.js`

---

## Defect classes

Each produced a wrong result that looked right. The count is how many times each
recurred, which is itself a measure of how well naming a thing prevents it.

| class | times | shape |
|---|---|---|
| `T-ONE-POINT` | 3 | Comparing two functions at a single input and concluding they are equal. Bit the mixed-TGATE test, the folded-vs-unfolded programs, and the TOP-vs-ADD comparison, where 81 of 19,683 tables matched at one pair. |
| `T-STALE-CONSTANT` | 5 | A hardcoded count in a test or a document going stale when the thing it counted grew. The closure test kept passing against an opcode list the source no longer had; test-findings.js miscounted its own prediction sets; and the README stated both a check total and a prediction tally that had drifted. The first two were fixed by deriving them. The third could not be owned by any one suite, because it is the sum of all of them, so run-all.js sums the suites and test-findings.js recomputes the tally. Fifth bite: the decode audit hardcoded the direct-encodable width as 6 in its cost section, two lines below the search that had just measured it as 5 -- so it printed a saving the measurement immediately above it had already refuted. The cost section now reads the search result. A constant is not safe merely because the thing it duplicates is nearby. Fifth bite, in a REGISTRATION rather than in prose about a result. AK1 typed A_27 = 27!/2 as a 25-digit number when it is 28 -- three zeros dropped, a factor of a thousand -- inside the commit that registered the prediction, where it could not be corrected afterwards without breaking the protocol. It cost nothing only because the tool COMPUTES the factorial and compares against that, rather than against the digits in the docstring, so the run verified the claim and the typed number was never load-bearing. AGENTS.md already says to derive constants and never hardcode them. The rule was obeyed in the code and broken in the sentence next to it, which is where it is easiest to break and hardest to notice. |
| `T-SILENT-NAN` | 1 | Writing through a missing label produced an undefined address, so the write silently did nothing. The core interpreter ran with no control register and no complaint. |
| `T-ADJACENCY` | 1 | .fold reading nine cells from a table that was shorter, silently borrowing whatever followed it. |
| `T-EXHAUSTED-NOT-CLOSED` | 3 | Confusing ran out of budget with finished. A search that exhausts its depth limit, one that hits its size cap, and one that genuinely closes are three different outcomes; conflating them produced a false negative verdict on V3. It recurred in the E sweep, where one counter held both settled-sooner-than-predicted and needed-longer-than-predicted, and the correctness check was skipped for the second bucket -- so an exhaustive claim was published while resting on an unmeasured decomposition. That time the numbers happened to be right: the second bucket was empty. Report the outcomes separately and check that they sum to the total. Third bite, this time in a CHECKER rather than an instrument: the staged solver was compared against solve() by crediting agreement only when both settled, so the cases where both agreed precisely that the network does NOT settle were counted as disagreements, and the tool declared its own results suspect. |
| `T-SOURCE-NOT-TERMINAL` | 1 | Switch-level reachability traversing THROUGH a driven node. A path from one rail that touches another rail and continues out of it makes correct circuits look contended. Rails and inputs are ideal sources and must terminate a path. |
| `T-INSTRUMENT-FALSE-VERDICT` | 21 | The measuring tool, not the thing measured, producing the failure. V3 read depth exhaustion as saturation; W2 traversed reachability through rails; X5 keyed a network by ordered terminals when D4 says terminals have no order; G4 dropped a qualifier that was present in its own registration and counted a quantity restated in a second set as colliding with itself. Each reported a verdict about the world that was a fact about the instrument. When a result contradicts a prediction, suspect the instrument first, and check the loop against the sentence that was registered. Fourth bite: the terminal audit held its storage cells with hold=LOW, which is the WRITE configuration -- the hold switches are n-types at threshold HIGH, so LOW opens the feedback loop and every cell floats. Every one of 81 cases in both families read Z, and the audit would have reported the roadmap blocking question as answered NO. A verdict of "nothing works" against a family that demonstrably works is the instrument. Fifth bite: the memory rig built its decoder with the first address trit MOST significant and its read tree with that trit LEAST significant. Each half was internally consistent; together they addressed different words for 18 of 27 addresses, so writes appeared to land in the wrong place and every read-back failed. Two halves of one address path disagreeing about endianness reads exactly like a broken circuit. Sixth bite: the interconnect rig named its sources `src0_0`, `src1_0`, ... and SEEDED them, without building anything behind them. A seed is an initial value, not a driver -- T5 says reachability starts at rails and only at rails -- so every source resolved to Z on pass one and stayed there. Both topologies routed Z, which read as "interconnect does not work at all" rather than "these are not sources". The same fact this repository already records as "an input gates but never sources", arriving in a form nobody recognised. Seventh bite, and inverted: a TEST CASE accused a correct instrument. The Schreier-Sims verification paired a 3-cycle with a 25-cycle and called the pair "A_27"; between them they move 25 of 27 points, so the tool returned 25!/2 -- exactly right for what was actually built -- and was scored WRONG. When a verification case fails, the case is as suspect as the thing it checks. Eighth bite: the sequencer rig called tAdderCell without its TAG, which names every internal node of the cells two tables. All three cells received the tag `undefined`, so their internal trees shared node names and merged into one circuit -- the incrementer resolved to unknown and the sequencer appeared to visit two states instead of twenty-seven. An omitted parameter that looks optional silently welded three circuits together. Ninth bite, in the same phase and pointing the other way: the handshake section counted the two driving values that DISABLE the loop as "settled cleanly", which would have reported a self-timed handshake as working on the strength of two circuits in which no handshake occurs. A false positive and a false negative from one tool in one run. Two more, found by reconciling this list against results/07-negative.md, which had one occurrence the manifest never named and lacked two the manifest did: the detector truth table hand-copied from a comment and INVERTED, which produced 36 failures out of 54 -- every one where the middle word disagreed with the selected word and none where they agreed, the exact signature real contention would leave, reading as the publishable headline that the decoded selector cannot read storage. Two views of one list drifted apart in opposite directions, which is what a second copy of a record is for and against. Twelfth bite: AB2s first erasure census folded the operand INTO the state, which is a defensible boundary and not the one AB2 asked about, so MIN read as a single fixed 4.5033 bits when the registered prediction was about a range from 0 to 9.5098 -- a correct computation about a different question, which would have recorded a prediction as FAILED when it held in full. Thirteenth bite, and it produced the most interesting wrong headline yet. AC1 detected whether a program reads input with a regex anchored at the start of the line, which misses every LABELLED instruction -- threeway.tasm carries "body: IN". So the audit reported a program that never reads input whose step count nonetheless varied with the input: a deterministic machine charging different amounts for data it never touches, which would have been the finding of the set. It was a broken parser standing next to an exported real one. Replaced with the assembler's own tokenizer, which moved the count of input-reading programs from five to eight and changed what AC1 was even about. Fourteenth bite, and it pointed the flattering way, which is the dangerous one. AD2's tabulator memoised only TERMINATING values, so each of the 366 divergent inputs walked its full three-thousand-step guard, learned nothing, and left the next divergent input to do it again: 1,098,362 evaluations to price 729 inputs. It reported a patient predictor as three hundred times WORSE than simply re-running, which is exactly the answer that would have made AD2 fail and the implied receipt look sound. Non-termination is an answer too, and a correct tabulator records it; walking until the path meets either a known value or itself resolves every state once and costs 728. An instrument that errs toward the hypothesis under test will not be caught by finding the result surprising, because it is not surprising. Fifteenth bite, and the SAME MECHANISM AS THE ELEVENTH in the same thread. AH2's reuse instrument walked every hailstone input to a 3,000-step guard, including the 366 that never terminate -- and those cycle through a handful of states three thousand times each, so hailstone measured 1,513x reuse against its true 10.43x. AD2's first tabulator failed for exactly this reason a few sets earlier and the repair was recorded there. A guard counted as work is apparently not a lesson that transfers by having been written down once; it has to be looked for. The repaired figure of 3,777 visits reproduces AD2's number exactly, which is the cross-check that says the two sets now measure one thing. Sixteenth bite, and a new flavour: MISREADING SOMEONE ELSE'S SPEC. AI1 implemented the Ladder's history operator with "SUM prev" read as the sum of everything so far INCLUDING the most recent term. That generates 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 -- the powers of two -- and agrees with Fibonacci at exactly one of forty terms, so the audit reported that an external artifact's central operator does not do what it says. The Ladder's own derivation line states the indexing unambiguously, L(n+1) = 1 + SUM L(0..n-1), so prev EXCLUDES the last term. One term short and the sequence changes species. Every earlier bite in this list was a wrong instrument pointed at this project's own subject; this one was a wrong instrument pointed at somebody else's finished work, where the failure mode is publishing a refutation of a thing you misread. Seventeenth bite, in AN: the shift attack wrapped a value that was already a value in val() a second time, shifting every nonce it produced by TRYTE_MIN. It reported solving 0 of 729 messages at the two hardest difficulties and looked entirely plausible on its own -- a structured puzzle that resists a structural attack is a perfectly sensible-sounding result. What caught it was the CONTRADICTION with AN3, which had measured 465 of those same messages as mineable by exhaustive search. The antibody is not a code review but a cross-check: the fast attack and the slow sweep must agree on WHICH messages are solvable, not merely produce numbers of a believable size. |
| `T-PREMISE-NOT-ANSWER` | 1 | A prediction failing on an assumption it never stated rather than on the quantity it asked about. X2 asked which seeds are self-consistent and assumed every seed resolves; two do not. The assumption, not the answer, was the falsifiable part. |
| `T-FAKE-RANDOM` | 1 | A sampling instrument that was not sampling. A seeded generator multiplied a 31-bit seed by a 31-bit constant, which overflows the 53 bits a JS number holds exactly, so the low-order bits it returned were rounding noise: three of its eight node names were drawn essentially never and no random network ever floated or contended. It looked like 400 trials and was closer to 400 repetitions of one. Random input needs a vacuity check on what it actually produced, not on how many times it ran. |
| `T-CHECK-FORBIDS-HEALTHY-STATE` | 2 | A consistency check that treated a legitimate intermediate state as a defect. It demanded that tools/ and the manifest prediction sets be equal in number; they are equal only between phases, because registering a tool predictions and recording its results are deliberately separate commits. During a registration there is one more tool than there are sets, and that is the protocol working. The check now names the pending tool instead of failing on it. Second bite: the design-folder status-marker check scanned for bare vocabulary words with a word boundary, and a new trap id -- T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE -- contains UNKNOWN between hyphens. The check failed a document whose vocabulary was entirely correct, because an identifier is not a marker. |
| `T-SEARCH-WHERE-A-CHECK-WOULD-DO` | 1 | An instrument that searched for a value it could have verified. Finding the exact pass count by scanning k = 1 upward cost up to eighty solves per input on a 1,776-switch network and did not finish inside ten minutes. The count is the same for every input, so it needs finding once and checking twice thereafter -- settles at k, does not settle at k-1. Two solves, not eighty. |
| `T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN` | 5 | A measured result stated as a property of the SUBJECT when it was a property of the DESIGN measured. Z2 swept buffer placements in one family of trees and concluded a depth floor for ternary at any price; a different selector beat it. E4, and Y2 and Z5 before it, measured raw-select circuits and concluded settling time is never data-dependent; a decoded selector made it data-dependent. Both times the numbers were right and the noun was too big. Before writing ternary, or this model, ask whether the sweep visited more than one design. Third bite, and the first scored against this project's own prose rather than against a sweep. AE2 and AE4 measured exactly one musical affordance -- the availability of transpositionally symmetric chords -- and the write-up headed the section "and here ternary is genuinely worse", generalising from one affordance to an entire art form. Consonance, rhythm, contour and timbre were untouched, and so was the distinction between ternary as a TUNING and ternary as an ADDRESSING scheme, which is the layer a 3x3 pad grid actually uses. The tell is the same every time: the sweep visited one thing and the sentence named a category. Ask what the sweep did NOT visit before choosing the noun. |
| `T-CENSUS-COUNTS-ITSELF` | 1 | A measurement over a corpus that the measurement is then written into. G4 surveyed the manifest for repeated integers, and recording its own result added those integers to the manifest a second time -- as the values it had excluded -- so the next run found them colliding and the prediction failed against its own record. Nothing was wrong with the world or the first answer. If a result is stored where it will later be read as data, exclude the storing record from the read, and derive the exclusion from something structural rather than an id. |
| `T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE` | 3 | A registered criterion whose verdict depends on run-to-run variation. H1 predicted a spread under 3x and measured 3.72 on one run and 2.89 on the next, either side of its own line, so the same world produced both a pass and a fail. The attempt to salvage a more robust shape from it flipped too. A threshold placed near the noise floor is a defect in the prediction rather than a fact about the subject; either widen it until it cannot flip, or measure the quantity and report it without asserting a bound. Second bite, and it was sitting inside the suite that records the first. test-headroom section 5 checked "the six-trit adder is sweepable inside an hour" against a LIVE timing. It passed on an idle machine and failed at 1.84 h inside a full suite run on a loaded one -- the same world returning both verdicts. Section 4 of the same file already refuses to assert durations and enforces that refusal by grepping itself; section 5 was quietly doing what section 4 forbids, four sections below the comment explaining why not to. The repair is the one the class prescribes: assert the RATIO, which survives any host -- a 50,000-device sweep costs about 80x a 624-device one -- and report the hour figures without checking them. On the loaded host the measured sweep budget is 335 devices against H2 recorded 4,806, so the figure was never a constant of nature and is now labelled as a measurement taken on a stated machine. Third bite, in AO1: a 5% band was registered around a null that 400 draws confirm exactly, but scored against ONE fixed pseudorandom map -- which turned out to sit 2.09 sigma out, while 336 of 400 draws would have passed. The criterion did not depend on run-to-run variation this time; it depended on WHICH SAMPLE WAS FROZEN AS THE CONTROL, which is the same defect seen from the other side. A single fixed pseudorandom object is one draw and a null model is a distribution; comparing them directly scores the seed rather than the claim. The remedy is to register the band against the control own empirical spread, or to sweep. |
| `T-TRANSCRIBED-TABLE` | 1 | A fact that could have been RUN was hand-copied instead. The terminal audit seeded a detector output from its truth table as written in a comment. The comment was right; the transcription inverted it, putting an n-type gate above its threshold so a selector leg conducted on exactly the addresses where it must be off. The result was not noise: 36 of 54 cases failed, every one of them a case where the middle word disagreed with the selected word and none where they agreed -- the exact mechanistic signature real contention would produce, and a plausible headline finding. A wrong instrument does not look wrong. When a value is derivable by running a two-line network, run it rather than copying it. |
| `T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE` | 1 | A control signal that is a COMPUTED node rather than a primary input is unknown on the first pass of the fixed point, and unknown conduction is treated as possible -- so on pass one it bridges or breaks everything it gates. Counted ONCE, not twice: B1a predicted exactly this shape for a decoded selector's middle leg in its own registration commit BEFORE the run, which is the protocol working rather than a trap anyone fell into. It bit in C, where nothing in the registration anticipated it: every hold gate in a 27-word array is a decoder output, and all 26 unaddressed words went to X on every write. The cells hold perfectly when hold is a primary input and not at all when it is a decoder output. The fix is not a workaround -- solve the control cone on its own and seed it. The general shape is that a circuit correct at its fixed point can be unreachable from a cold start, and the larger the control fan-out the more it takes with it. |
| `T-SCOPE-DECIDES-THE-VERDICT` | 4 | A correct computation scored a prediction wrongly because the measurement drew its state boundary somewhere the prediction did not. N1 asked whether a BUILD puts MID on a node when the registered rule was whether the FUNCTION requires it, and scored the detector FORCED while the next section built the same function with zero taps. AB2's first census folded the operand into the state, which is a defensible boundary and not the one AB2 asked about, so MIN came out as a single fixed figure while the clauses spoke of a range, and AB2 would have been recorded as FAILED. Both readings are defensible and the registration did not say which it meant, so the honest diagnosis is an ambiguous registration as much as a mis-scoped instrument. The defence is to state the boundary in the registration and to report every reading the question admits rather than one. Third bite, and this one arrived from a LATER set rather than from the instrument itself. G4 censuses the manifest for integers appearing in both the vocabulary half and the circuit half; its classifier returns a third value, other, for a tool requiring neither, and the crossing test counted other as a side. Set AB then recorded 19,683 -- the size of the two-input tritwise function space, which Q also holds -- and a set belonging to NEITHER half read as crossing between them. The computation was correct and the question was not the registered one. Scoped to the two named halves, which is a structural exclusion rather than an id. Fourth bite, and the registration had stated the boundary CORRECTLY. AG1's docstring said a tabulator indexes what varies between runs of the same program, and that a program's own instructions are identical every run and cost it nothing -- then the code poisoned every cell of the assembled image and counted whatever moved the price. That measures the program rather than the input, so interp-core came out at 73 live words and all nine programs cleared AD4's threshold: a result that would have reported an implied receipt as already working here. Naming a class does not stop you walking into it. Once the definition is written down the only place the gap can hide is between the docstring and the code, so that is where to look. |
| `T-TOOL-CHECKED-ONLY-BY-IMPORT` | 1 | A tool that is exercised only through require(), so the path it takes when actually RUN is never covered. The erasure audit was made silent on import by a mechanical rename of every console.log call to log -- which rewrote the body of log itself into a call to itself. The tool crashed with a stack overflow on every single run, and every check in its suite stayed green, because a test that imports the module sets MAIN false and no print path ever executes. Nothing about the numbers was wrong; the program was simply broken in the half nobody looked at. The antibody is a check that spawns the tool as a subprocess and asserts it exits cleanly and printed every section, made affordable by an environment variable that caps its most expensive sweep. Mutation-tested: reintroducing the recursive definition turns all three of those checks red. |
| `T-CONTROL-CANNOT-DISCRIMINATE` | 2 | A control that cannot fail, because the parameter the claim is about cancels out of it. Set AQ's control gave its two cost terms the same pseudorandom draw, so the exchange rate factored out and its optimum was constant in exactly the dimension the sweep was measuring -- it could only ever agree, whatever the trees did. The antibody is to check the control's RESPONSIVENESS before reading its verdict: the suite now asserts that the registered control is invariant in gamma at all 45 leaf counts, so the defect is recorded as a fact rather than left looking like evidence, and a second control with independent draws carries the discriminating work. |
